title: Why churn diagnostics miss the real problem when a business is stuck near 100k
hook: If your business is stuck near 100k, the first place to look is who the funnel is bringing in.
caption:
If your business is stuck near 100k and you cannot tell why, the first place to look is the kind of customer you are attracting.

Most growth teams at this size run an onboarding review. They look at where the new user drops off. They look at how fast the first click happens. They rewrite the welcome email.

These are real levers. They are also the wrong place to start.

Two customers can sign up the same week and take your business in opposite directions. One pays once and disappears. One pays again, brings a teammate, and stays three years. Same funnel. Same price. Different kind of buyer.

The second kind is what turns 100k into 500k. Every business near 100k I have looked at is short on that second kind.

Here is a cleaner diagnostic than any retention dashboard.

Pull every signup from 90 days ago. Count how many are still active today. Count how many paid more this month than the month they signed up. Count how many brought someone new in.

Those three numbers tell you what kind of business you are running. Not the lifetime value report. Not the monthly revenue chart. Those three numbers.

If the count is low, the fix is not a better welcome email. The fix is further upstream, in how the offer is described, who it is described to, and what promise is made on the page that pulls them in.

title: The two types of customers that decide whether your business crosses 100k
hook: Here is how to tell if your business will stall at 100k. Look at the kind of lead you are attracting. Not the number. The kind.
tweets:
Here is how to tell if your business will stall at 100k.

Look at the kind of lead you are attracting. Not the number. The kind.

Two leads can look the same on day 1 and pull your business in opposite directions by day 90.

A low-quality lead signs up, clicks around, never comes back. They collected you the way they collect tabs. You were one of forty tools they tried this quarter.

A high-quality lead signs up, builds something with you, brings a teammate in by month two.

If you are near 100k and growth has flattened, three questions:

1. Of the leads from last quarter, how many are still active today?
2. Of those, how many pay more now than when they started?
3. Of those, how many brought someone else in?

A high-quality lead is not the one with the biggest first purchase. It is the one whose second, third, and fourth purchase add up to more than the first.

Retention is where margin lives. Everyone knows this. Almost nobody measures for it.

High-quality leads come in through three doors. A clear promise. A specific problem. A reason the buyer cannot solve it somewhere cheaper.

Vague landing pages pull vague leads. Sharp landing pages pull sharp leads. Your headline is doing the sorting.

Three things a high-quality lead needs from you in the first 14 days.

1. A small win they can feel.
2. A second use case that connects to the first.
3. A reason to come back on their own, not because you pinged them.

Pull your signups from 90 days ago. Mark the ones still active. Mark the ones who pay more now than they did then.

That second list is your real business. Everything else is noise you have been paying to acquire.

title: The most common reason a 100k business thinks it has a churn problem
hook: Borrowed-credibility Reddit observation: the churn is the second problem, not the first.
caption:
I have been reading threads on r/SaaS this week. One came up twice.

A founder is stuck near 100k a year. They have been told they have a churn problem. They spend three months rewriting onboarding. Nothing moves.

The pattern I keep noticing is different. The churn is not the first problem. It is the second problem.

The first problem is who the funnel brought in.

People who jump between ten tools a month will keep jumping. A better onboarding flow does not make that person stay. It only delays the day they leave.

So before I touch onboarding for a client in this spot, I do one thing. I pull the last 300 signups and look at which ones came back in the second week. That one number changes the whole read.

If it is low, onboarding is not the first move. The first move sits one step before the sign up.

title: The Creative Strategy Upskilling Path for 2026
hook: If you can write good copy, you can do creative strategy. You just need to add a few other skills.
caption:
If you can write good copy, you can do creative strategy. You just need to add a few other skills.

This is the thing nobody tells people getting into creative strategy from a copywriting background. The writing itself is not the bottleneck. Every halfway decent copywriter already researches, studies the market, and thinks about offers.

The gap is everywhere else.

Reading data from ad accounts. Knowing how an ad gets made, not just written. Leading a small team, even if that team is one junior copywriter and one video editor. Spotting a winning ad inside a sea of losing ones. Talking to a client about results without turning the call into a status update.

A copywriter is hired to write. A creative strategist is hired to decide. Most of the work is upstream of the words.

The writing is the easy part for most people trying to make this move. The hard part is learning to sit in the decision chair.

Here is a pattern I have seen across the creative-strategy community for the last few years.

Someone good at writing copy books a few projects. They charge five hundred, maybe a thousand. The client pays, the project wraps, the writer moves on to the next one. Every month looks the same. Every month ends with a quiet "next month I will charge more." Next month rarely does.

The move that changes the picture is not a pricing course.

It is the thing being sold.

A copywriter is hired to write the words. A creative strategist is hired to decide what the ad should do, who it should talk to, and why that promise will work against what the market is already running.

Two very different sales conversations.

One starts with "Hi, I write Facebook ads. Here are samples." It ends in a five-hundred dollar project if the client likes your taste.

The other starts with "I looked at your current ads. The winning one is winning for X. The rest are losing because Y. Here is what I would test next week. I can run the whole thing." It ends in a retainer.

Same writer. Different job. The second one is a creative strategist. The ceiling is higher because the role is higher.

title: Why 100k is the most dangerous milestone for a growing business
hook: 100k feels like the top of the climb. For a lot of businesses, it is the start of the hardest stretch.
caption:
100k feels like the top of the climb. For a lot of businesses, it is the start of the hardest stretch.

Here is the pattern I keep seeing in the first year across SaaS, coaching, and small e-commerce.

Months one to twelve, you stitch something together that a handful of people truly want. Word gets around. Revenue climbs. You cross 100k and celebrate. You post it. You plan the next hire. You sign a longer lease.

Months thirteen to eighteen, the numbers stop cooperating.

Tools that were cheap get more expensive because the customer uses them more. The price you set when the product was bare has not moved. The easy traffic channel you rode up has filled with copycats. Growth has slowed, not from any one thing, from all of them at once.

The fix is rarely a new ad campaign or a new feature.

Three places to look first.

1. The cost to serve your heaviest customer, in plain dollars, this month.
2. The share of customers from a year ago who are still with you and still paying.
3. The promise on your landing page, read by a stranger, and whether it still sorts for the buyer you want.

Businesses at this stage rarely need to grow faster. They need the numbers underneath the growth to make sense.

title: 5 signs you are attracting the wrong customer at 100k
hook: A low-quality lead and a high-quality lead look the same on day 1. By day 30, one of them funds the business. The other quietly drains it.
tweets:
A low-quality lead and a high-quality lead look the same on day 1.

By day 30, one of them funds the business. The other quietly drains it.

Here are 5 telltales that show up in the first week, no matter what you sell.

1. What they do after the first small win.

Low-quality: done, closes the tab, moves on.

High-quality: uses the product for a second thing, same week. This second use is the single earliest signal that the buyer will stay.

2. How they talk about you.

Low-quality: "I tried a tool for that."

High-quality: "I use this for X." The first is a mention. The second is a habit forming. If your customer cannot name you in one sentence, the offer is not clear enough.

3. Who they tell.

Low-quality: nobody.

High-quality: a teammate, a friend, a peer in the same field. The referral does not need to be formal. It shows up as a message, a screenshot, a forwarded link. Watch for it.

4. Whether they complain.

Low-quality: silent, then gone.

High-quality: sends feedback, asks questions, wants a feature. Complaining is a form of investment. The customer who emails you is the one you want to keep.

5. Whether they come back without a nudge.

Low-quality: comes back only when you email or advertise.

High-quality: comes back on their own, inside the first 14 days, to solve a different problem with the same thing they bought. This is the line between a buyer and a customer.

Pull last month's new buyers. Mark the ones who hit any two of the five above. Spend your time on that group.

The group that missed all five was never your audience. They cost you money. You were paying to find the other list.

title: How to Land Your First Client Without a Portfolio
hook: How to land creative strategy clients without a portfolio.
caption:
How to land creative strategy clients without a portfolio.

I have worked online for several years, and before that in corporate marketing roles. Nobody has ever asked me for a portfolio. Not once. Every person who has hired me, online or off, asked me to think about their business on a call, or to send something in writing about what I would do.

A portfolio is nice to have. It is not the thing that gets you hired.

Here is what does.

A breakdown of the prospect's current work. One of their ads, their landing page, their welcome sequence. What you see, what you would change, what you would test next.

A one-page document written for their offer before they ever hire you. Who it is for. Why it is selling now. What you would push harder on.

A short screen recording walking them through the first three moves you would make if they signed a retainer tomorrow.

All three show the prospect the one thing they actually care about. Can this person think about my business.

The creative strategists who stay stuck are the ones who will not send anything unsolicited. The ones who get hired do it anyway.

title: First Client Without Portfolio (FB Page)
hook: I spend time in communities of people trying to move from copywriting into creative strategy, and there is one pattern that comes up every week.
caption:
I spend time in communities of people trying to move from copywriting into creative strategy, and there is one pattern that comes up every week.

Someone says they cannot get clients because they do not have a portfolio. When you ask what they actually sent the prospect, it is a services page. Nothing else.

Portfolios are not the problem. The services page is not the problem either. The problem is that the prospect just got eighteen other messages like it that week. Every one of them looked the same.

What gets a reply is proof the sender thought about the prospect's business before reaching out.

Try this for your next ten outreach messages.

1. Pick a prospect whose ads you have actually looked at this week.
2. Screenshot one ad they are running.
3. Write three sentences. What you would test changing. Why. What you think would happen.
4. Send that as your first message. No services page. No rate. No ask.

That reads like a piece of thinking, not a pitch. Out of ten messages sent this way, some percentage reply. Some percentage of those turn into a paid conversation.

Nobody I have worked with in the last few years asked me for a portfolio. They asked me what I thought. This is the same thing, in writing, sent first.

title: 14 retention levers for businesses near 100k and the 3 that move the needle
hook: 14 ways to keep more of the customers you already have. Business owners at 100k know three and use one.
caption:
14 ways to keep more of the customers you already have.

Business owners at 100k often know three of these and use one. The other eleven sit untouched.

Here is the full list, ranked from the highest return on effort down.

1. The first 14 days after the purchase. This is where most loss happens. Fix this and the rest gets easier.
2. Sorting your customers by who buys the most, most recently. Spending your time on that group.
3. Pricing that moves as the habit forms. Annual plans that save real money. Small paid add-ons.
4. Email to people who already bought, not to fill a list.
5. A small community, even a private chat, around the product.
6. A referral reason that rewards the customer and the friend.
7. Support that reaches out first, before the customer complains.
8. Stories and reviews from customers told in their own words.
9. A personalised next step inside the product that matches the user.
10. Reminders in the right channel, not every channel.
11. A direct line on chat for the customers who pay the most.
12. A letter in the post for the customers who pay even more than that.
13. A short text message when something time-sensitive matters.
14. A workflow that mixes the product with a human hand, even once a month.

You do not need fourteen. You need three, done well.

The first three move the most weight. The first one more than the other two combined.

title: 14 Retention Levers (X Thread)
hook: 14 ways to keep more of the customers you already have. The first three move the most weight. The other eleven fill in around them.
tweets:
14 ways to keep more of the customers you already have.

Businesses near 100k often know three of these and use one. The first three on this list move the most weight. The other eleven fill in around them.

Swipe the thread.

Lever 1. The first 14 days after the purchase.

Most of the loss lives here. The first two weeks decide whether the buyer becomes a customer or a refund. Fix this before any other channel.

Lever 2. Sort your customers by who pays the most, most recently.

Not every customer counts the same. The top slice is worth ten times the bottom half. Plenty of business owners do not know who is in that top slice.

Lever 3. Price that moves with the habit.

An annual plan that saves real money. A small paid add-on that fits the habit. A price that goes up for heavy users, not new ones. Price is not only for the first sale.

Lever 4. Email to people who already bought.

Not a big list. A list of buyers. Two emails a week, written by a person, will beat any automation sent to a cold list.

Lever 5. A small community, even a private chat.

Customers stay longer when they know other customers. One line of conversation a day is enough. It does not need to scale.

Lever 6. A referral reason that rewards both sides.

Not a generic link. A reason that fits how the buyer already talks about you. The reward should feel fair, not like a trick.

Lever 7. Support that reaches first.

A check-in before the complaint. Five minutes of your time on day ten earns a year of the customer's.

Lever 8. Stories in the customer's words.

A raw quote, a screenshot, a voice note. Not a polished case study. The rough version is what gets read.

Levers 9 to 14.

1. A next step inside the product that fits this customer.
2. Reminders in one channel, not every channel.
3. A chat line for the heaviest buyers.
4. A letter in the post for the biggest.
5. A short text when time matters.
6. A workflow where a human checks in once a month.

Three running well beats fourteen running half way. Audit which of the first three you are missing before you add a fourteenth.

title: LI Second Post: How to use pricing as a retention lever
hook: How to use price to keep more of the customers you already have.
caption:
How to use price to keep more of the customers you already have.

Businesses at this size often set a price once when they launch, and change it only when a customer renews. Price is treated like a shop sign. Stick it up, leave it alone.

Three things businesses near 100k can try instead.

1. Raise the price for the feature your best customers actually use. Not for new customers. For the ones already heavy on it. They will pay it. They have already built a habit.
2. Offer an annual plan that saves real money. Not five percent. Something the customer feels. It pulls the decision out of the monthly second-guessing.
3. Add a small paid add-on that fits the habit. Something small, useful, and tied to the thing they come back for. Not a bundle. One clean add.

The point of price is not only to sign the customer up. It is to give a reason to stay another year.

Thread on what moved.

Where we started.

Standard broadcasts going to everyone on the list on the same day. Open rates looked fine. Revenue was flat. The list was being shouted at, not written to.

First move. Split the list into three groups based on behaviour, not size.

Group A bought in the last three months.
Group B bought six to eighteen months ago and had gone quiet.
Group C had never bought but still opened emails.

Group A is the easiest group to underpay attention to, because they already pay you.

We sent them an early access email twenty-four hours before anything public. It read as a thank-you, not a promotion. Revenue from this group doubled first.

Group B needed a specific reason to come back. Not "we miss you."

A new product that matched something they bought before. One sentence. One link. It brought back a real slice of the group.

Group C needed the cleanest offer. One hook. One clear saving. Four emails through the window with rising urgency.

Accept that some of this group never buys and write for the ones who will.

Send times mattered more than subject lines.

Each group got a different send time that matched when their past opens had landed. No clever trick. Just reading what the data already said.

Result. Revenue per lead almost doubled over the window [verify with Muddassir: exact figure].

Most of the lift came from Group A, at the smallest send volume. The list we had was bigger than we were treating it.

title: How to do cold outreach as a creative strategist and stand out
hook: Why cold outreach is still worth your time, even in 2026.
caption:
Why cold outreach is still worth your time, even in 2026.

Here is how I think about it. In my first year online I ran more than twenty million cold emails [verify with Muddassir: exact figure]. That is why I never needed to build a big audience first. Never starved for leads. Never slid into DMs for "networking."

Most people today will tell you cold outreach hurts your brand. My take is the opposite. If a creative strategist needs cold outreach, it usually means they do not have budget for anything else, no leverage in the market yet, and no real brand built. A brand that does not exist cannot be hurt.

Done right, cold outreach is a volume game. If you cannot play volume, do not attempt it. If you can, it is the fastest way to prove to yourself that you can start and hold a conversation with a stranger. That skill does not go away.

What cold outreach built for me.

Hundreds of booked calls a month in that first year. Hundreds of tests on a single sentence. A rapport with strangers that let me ask for high-ticket work on the first call, because the first impression was never "please hire me." It was "here is what I see in your business."

What I would tell a creative strategist starting today. If you can run Facebook ads for yourself, that is probably a cleaner road to the same outcome. If you cannot, run cold outreach. Send messages that are not pitches. Send a piece of thinking about their business. No rate. No ask. No services page.

Ten sent properly gets a handful of replies. A handful of replies gets a paid conversation.

It is not new. It is over fifty years old. I have seen very few businesses near 100k use it, even though it costs nothing to set up and explains most of what retention does and does not move.

Here is why it matters.

Your customers are not all worth the same. Some buy every week. Some buy twice a year. Two customers can look active on a chart and pull your business in opposite directions. You do not know which is which until you rank them by those three things.

Spotify spends a fortune on data science. They did not invent this. They used what was already there.

title: The retention problem every business faces near 100k
hook: At 100k, the revenue line looks fine. The problem is never how many leave. It is who stays.
caption:
# The retention problem for businesses near 100k

## What the chart does not tell you

At 100k, the revenue line looks fine. Each month is a little bigger than the last. Refunds stay below ten percent. Churn hovers in the single digits. If you close the laptop and look at the room, nothing feels like it is on fire.

Compound a small monthly loss over eighteen months, and you have quietly replaced more than half of your customer base. The top-line growth hides it because new customers are coming in a little faster than old ones are leaving. The day that gap narrows, which it always does, the picture changes in an afternoon.

## The real question is not how many leave, it is who stays

Two customers sign up the same week. One pays once and disappears. One pays, comes back, buys again, brings a teammate. Same product. Same price. Different kind of buyer.

The business at 100k that stalls is the one filling up with the first kind. The business at 100k that breaks through is the one slowly tilting the list toward the second.

You will not tell them apart on day one. You will tell them apart on day ninety. That is the day the business you actually have becomes visible.

## Why most teams look in the wrong place

When customers leave, most teams rewrite onboarding. They add a product tour. They test subject lines. They hire a growth engineer.

None of this changes the kind of customer coming through the door. The leverage is earlier, in the sentence on the landing page, in the promise on the ad, in what the business says it is for.

A vague promise pulls vague customers. A sharp promise pulls sharp customers. The copy is doing the sorting whether you want it to or not.

## What to look at this week

Pull your last ninety days of customers. Count how many are still with you today. Count how many pay more now than when they started. Count how many brought someone new in.

Those three counts are your business. Not the monthly revenue chart. Not the customer count. Those three.

If the counts are low, the fix is not further downstream. It is further upstream.

## Three moves that work for any business near 100k

**One. Rewrite the first sentence on your landing page.**

Read it cold. Would a stranger know, in one line, who it is for and what it solves? If not, rewrite that line before anything else. Every other channel feeds off it.

**Two. Pay closer attention to the customers you already have.**

Sort your list by who paid the most, most recently. The top ten percent is where most of the money lives. A short call, a direct message, an annual plan that saves them real money, a small add-on that fits their habit. These are where retention gets built, one customer at a time.

**Three. Fill the first two weeks after a sale.**

Most businesses near 100k leave that window empty. One welcome email, then silence. A customer who just paid is the most open to hearing from you they will ever be. A real sequence in those two weeks carries the next three months.

## What happens if you do nothing

The revenue line keeps climbing for a while. The gap between signups and losses narrows, quarter by quarter. One month the gap closes. The line flattens. The team does not know why.

That is the retention problem for businesses near 100k. It is slow and then it is fast, and it is almost always diagnosed after it has already cost a year.

## What to do if you are here now

Pull the three counts this week. Look at them honestly. Rewrite the landing page line. Fill the two-week window. Start with the top ten percent of customers and work down.

Here is the move that changes your copy more than any course on frameworks. Pick one ad from a competitor you would like to work with. Spend twenty minutes on it. Not scrolling. Not screenshotting. Reading.

Four questions.

Four. What would you test next, if you ran this account tomorrow. One specific thing. Your hypothesis on the result.

Two. What is the promise in the first three seconds. Not what the brand is selling. What the ad is saying it will give the viewer. Name it in one sentence.

Three. What did the brand do to make the promise believable. A face on camera. A before and after. A customer quote. A stat. A mechanism. Name the move.

Four. What would you test next if you ran this account. Not what you would critique. What you would try. One specific change. Your guess on what would happen.

If you answer those four on every ad you save, inside a month you have a folder that looks like a strategy document. You will also find that your own hooks get easier to write.

title: What actually keeps customers with your business at 100k
hook: What keeps a customer at a business near 100k is not the feature list. It is what the customer has built inside what they bought from you.
caption:
What keeps a customer at a business near 100k.

It is not the feature list. It is not the price. It is what the customer has built inside what they bought from you.

Six months of their own history in the product. A way of using it that fits their week. A teammate they brought in. A third tool that now talks to yours.

A customer with all four of those is not leaving next quarter, even if a cheaper option shows up. A customer with none of them is one email away from trying something else.

Most businesses near 100k spend their week trying to add one more feature. They should spend the week making the customer's investment stick.

Three questions to ask this month.

1. On day thirty, what does a good customer have inside the product that they did not have on day one?
2. On day ninety, what have they set up that would take a day to rebuild somewhere else?
3. On day one hundred eighty, who else have they brought in?

If the answers are thin, the customer is thin. If the answers are specific, the customer is yours.

title: What actually keeps a customer at a business near 100k
hook: What keeps a customer at a business near 100k is rarely what you think. It is the history they have built inside what they bought from you.
tweets:
What keeps a customer at a business near 100k is rarely what you think.

It is not the feature list. It is not the price. It is the history they have built inside what they bought from you.

Thread on how to protect that, and what happens when you do not.

A customer on day thirty has almost nothing to lose by leaving. A customer on day one eighty has built a week around you, pulled a teammate in, and taught three other tools to talk to yours.

Those two customers look identical on a revenue report. They behave nothing alike.

The five things that hold a customer at month six.

Their own data inside the product. A habit that lives on a weekday. A teammate who also uses it. A tool it now connects to. A saved template or view that only makes sense to them.

Score your top twenty customers against those five. One point each. Maximum of five.

Most businesses near 100k find their top twenty average two. That is not a loyalty problem. That is a design problem. The product never asked the customer to put anything down.

What moves the score up.

Small templates the customer names themselves. A second user invited by the first. A third tool that writes into yours automatically. A weekly step the customer now does on a specific day.

What does not move the score up.

A better landing page. A louder email. A new feature the competition also ships next week. A discount. A webinar. A push notification the customer did not ask for.

The same design that holds customers also pulls in the kind of customer worth holding.

A product that expects investment sorts out the casual buyer before they ever pay. You stop paying to acquire people who were never going to stay anyway.

Which of the five is weakest in your business? Reply with a number one to five.

title: How to Use Meta Ad Library Like a Creative Strategist
hook: The Meta Ad Library is not a swipe file. Used well, it is a research tool that beats every other source for speed and accuracy.
caption:
How to use the Meta Ad Library as a creative strategist.

The Ad Library is not a swipe file. Used well, it is a research tool that beats every other source for speed and accuracy. Used badly, it is a hook-farm where copywriters copy a first line, paste it into their own ad, and then wonder why it did not convert.

Here is the scan that works. Five steps. Twenty minutes.

One. Filter by the last ninety days. Sort by start date. The ads running now are the ads worth looking at. Ignore the dead ones.

Two. Look for age. An ad that has run for more than sixty days is almost certainly working. The brand would have killed it otherwise. Write those brand names down.

Three. Look across versions. A brand running four variants of the same ad is testing. The variant still running after three weeks is the winner. That is your data point, not a random screenshot.

Four. Pull the angle, not the hook. What is the actual argument the ad is making. The hook is the delivery. The angle is the claim underneath it. Write the claim in one sentence.

Five. Note what is missing. The angle nobody in the category is running. The channel nobody is trying. The promise nobody is making. That gap is where your own ad goes.

For every winning ad, note five things on one page. Angle. Mechanism. Proof. Call to action. Emotional frame.

Ten ads through this on a Sunday and you have a mental model most creative strategists never build. It is the one thing that lets you walk into a call and answer what the brand should test next, not what a course taught you last year.
